description: We're a team of cadets from Kharkiv National University of Internal Affairs (Ukraine), passionate about programming and cybersecurity, from pentesting to building our own tools. We learn fast, work hard and want to ship a working project by the end of the hackathon.
summary:
CrewPulse is an offline-first Android app that lets astronauts run a quick self-exam, see the status of 
each body system at a glance and know what to do, even when Earth is up to 22 minutes away. It tracks 
ten indicators, from blood pressure, heart rate, sleep and reaction time to radiation dose and the WHO
5 well-being index, and compares every reading with clinical and NASA limits and with the astronaut's 
own baseline. Heart rate can also be measured with the phone camera. EWMA and CUSUM trend 
detection warn about gradual changes before a threshold is crossed. Findings are linked to nine NASA 
Human Research Program risks; triage takes the communication delay into account, and a compact 
report for the flight surgeon shows when Earth can answer. Real NASA DONKI space-weather data 
drives spacewalk GO / NO-GO, and a Digital Twin projects bone, muscle and radiation dose for ISS and 
Mars missions against NASA-STD-3001 limits and computes how much exercise is needed to stay 
within them. Every threshold links to its source. CrewPulse is a research prototype, not a medical device; 
demo astronaut data is synthetic
details:
Try it. Android APK (release v0.1.0): https://github.com/cybersecuritykali958-bot/nasa-space-apps/releases/tag/v0.1.0. Code, science sources and documentation: https://github.com/cybersecuritykali958-bot/nasa-space-apps

What it does. CrewPulse is an offline-first Android app for astronaut self-monitoring. The crew member signs in with an NFC badge and sees four tabs: Daily Operations (mission day, qualification level and continuity, a status row that lists which systems need attention, alerts and today's measurement protocol), Physiological Status (a holographic 3D body where each organ shows its system's status, plus a Digital Twin projection), Fitness for Duty (readiness for a spacewalk or landing, triage, space weather and a report for Earth) and Crew Member Profile. The daily check-in covers blood pressure, resting heart rate, fasting glucose, body temperature, sleep and mood, with an optional WHO-5 well-being test; heart rate can be measured with the phone camera, and a 3-minute reaction-time test (PVT) checks alertness.

How it works. Each reading is checked twice: against a population or NASA limit and against the astronaut's personal baseline (yellow at 15 %, red at 30 % deviation); the worse result wins. EWMA (Roberts 1959; Lucas & Saccucci 1990) and CUSUM (Page 1954) catch slow drifts before a limit is reached. Pattern rules combine indicators, for example temperature plus heart rate for a possible infection. Triage compares the time Earth needs to answer with the urgency of the finding, so on Mars the app switches to the onboard protocol. NASA DONKI solar particle events, coronal mass ejections and X-class flares feed the space-weather gate for spacewalks.

Digital Twin and countermeasure coach. The twin models hip bone density, leg strength and cumulative dose for a 6-month ISS mission, a Mars mission and the current environment, with and without exercise, and marks values beyond 14.4 months as extrapolation. The coach solves the inverse problem: the smallest share of the ARED exercise protocol that keeps bone and muscle within NASA-STD-3001 limits until the end of the mission. For 6 months on the ISS it needs 97 % to stay green and 56 % to stay out of red; for a full Mars mission even 100 % is not enough.

Report for Earth. One tap builds a compact plain-text packet for the flight surgeon (about 800 bytes: off-nominal values, trends, triage, space weather) and shows the one-way signal delay, the earliest possible reply and a countdown. In the prototype the downlink is simulated; the same text can be shared over any real channel.

Well-being and camera pulse. Besides the daily 1-5 mood rating, the app includes the WHO-5 Well-Being Index (World Health Organization 2024): five statements about the last two weeks, scored 0-100 %, with the published cut-off below 50 % (Topp et al. 2015). Camera pulse uses contact photoplethysmography: the fingertip covers the camera and the flash, and the heart rate is taken from the periodicity of the red channel with a signal-quality check; the result is saved as an estimated value.

Validation. Replayed day by day on a synthetic 180-day mission, the engine caught 10 of 14 events, 5 of them before the threshold with a mean lead of 16.6 days, and raised 6 false alarms across 9 indicators. The Digital Twin gives -3 % hip bone density for 6 months on the ISS with exercise, matching the -3 % femoral-neck average reported for recent ISS crews. The coach thresholds match a hand calculation from the model formulas, and the pulse algorithm recovers 48-170 bpm within 2 bpm on synthetic signals; 63 unit tests cover the engine and the new features.

Benefits and impact. Long missions cannot rely on real-time support from Earth. CrewPulse gives the crew an explainable first assessment: which indicators, why, and what to do next. Every threshold in the app links to its source, and values the team derived are marked as such. Daily measurement plans adapt to the astronaut's status, and a gamified protocol (qualification level, compliance points, continuity, commendations) supports adherence.

Tools. Kotlin, Jetpack Compose with Material 3, Navigation Compose, Room, WorkManager (reminders), CameraX (camera pulse) and kotlinx.serialization on Android; Python for demo data generation, the Digital Twin reference model, the NASA DONKI fetcher and rendering of the 3D body sprites (numpy, pillow; procedural, no external 3D model). Data lives in JSON files with sources attached. The app runs offline and is available in English, Ukrainian, German and Japanese.

Use of AI tools. The team used Claude Code and Cursor to write code and documentation and to check scientific sources; team members reviewed every change before merging. No AI-generated images, video or audio are used; the 3D body is rendered procedurally by our own script.

Limitations. CrewPulse is a research prototype, not a medical device, and it does not replace a flight surgeon. The demo astronaut is synthetic: 180 days of data generated from published rates of change and labelled as synthetic in the app. Most thresholds are terrestrial clinical references (AHA, ADA, CDC, NEWS2, AASM); spaceflight-specific limits are used where NASA publishes them (NASA-STD-3001 for radiation dose, bone density and muscle strength). The daily mood rating is a screening question; WHO-5 is validated in English, while our Ukrainian, German and Japanese wording is not an official validated translation. The reaction-time test reports mean response time, which is less sensitive to sleep loss than lapse counts. Camera pulse has been checked only on synthetic signals, not on people. The Digital Twin assumes losses scale linearly with gravity and has no human data for Moon or Mars gravity. The smartwatch and the downlink to Earth are simulated in the demo.
